newsitem.title: HUNGARY: E.Europe needs strict fiscal policies - conference.
newsitem.headline: E.Europe needs strict fiscal policies - conference.

text.p: Inflation rates between 10 and 30 percent in transition economies can be cut only with tight fiscal policies and deep structural and price adjustments, an international seminar held in Hungary heard this week.
Central bankers and finance ministry officials from eastern Europe, representatives of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and economists took part in the discussions, which ended on Tuesday.
IMF Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer told a news conference following the seminar that the negative impact of double-digit annual inflation outweighed the costs of reducing it.
"There are very big costs of staying with moderate inflation (of 10 to 30 percent)," he said.
Fischer said the conference had been optimistic over the prospects for central European countries, which plan to join the European Union (EU) over the next five years.

By the time the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland become EU members, they are likely to be in a good position concerning inflation provided their economic policies are "serious and disciplined", he added.
Inflation in April ran at 6.7 percent in the Czech Republic, 15.3 percent in Poland and 18.6 percent in Hungary.

Fischer said Hungary had taken serious steps in economic adjustment and inflation reduction recently and the government's plans to reduce inflation by four to five percent in both 1997 and 1998 were considered realistic at the conference.
"To bring the inflation down by four to five percent a year... would be impressive," he said.
Hungary targets inflation levels of 16 to 17 percent for the end of this year and and 13 to 14 percent for December 1998.
